Photo taken after the March 12, 1928 collapse of the Saint Francis Dam; this disastrous civil engineering failure cost over 600 lives in the resulting flood and brought the end of William Mulholland's career as the chief engineer of the Los Angeles Bureau of Water Works and Supply.

stills.file: St. Francis Dam after the 1928 failure.jpg
stills.categories: Sierra Pelona Ridge|St. Francis Dam|PD USGS
stills.description: St. Francis Dam Flood March 12-13, 1928, Los Angeles County, California. Taken from the same location as photo sht00664 , showing the remains of the dam and reservoir floor. The dam failed at 11:58:30 p.m. Monday March 12, 1928. The left (west) abutment of the dam was entirely swept away and the inactive San Francisquito Fault is clearly visible, being located along the contact zone of schist and conglomerate.

stills.categories: United States Geological Survey|St. Francis Dam|PD USGS|Files uploaded by PDTillman
stills.description: St. Francis Dam Flood March 12-13, 1928, Los Angeles County, California. Huge concrete block from the west abutment of the dam about half a mile below the dam. The block is approximately 63 feet long, 30 feet high, and 54 feet wide. Note the dam wing wall in the distance. March 17, 1928.

stills.categories: PD US not renewed|St. Francis Dam|Photographs in the Los Angeles Public Library|Template Unknown (author)
stills.description: St. Francis Dam in San Francisquito Canyon near Saugus was completed in 1926 and failed in 1928. It was part of the Owens Valley Aqueduct System. This post-failure photograph shows a view of the only remaining standing section and portions of the collapsed dam which had been part the eastern side .

stills.description: The iceberg suspected of having sunk the RMS Titanic , photographed by the chief steward of the liner Prinz Adalbert on the morning of April 15, 1912, just a few miles south of where Titanic sank. The steward had not yet heard about Titanic' s sinking, and he noticed the smear of what appeared to be red paint along the base of the iceberg, suggesting it had collided with a ship sometime in the previous 12 hours. Other accounts indicated that there were several icebergs in the vicinity of Titanic' s collision.
